name: Elena Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Elena, thanks for joining. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, party or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the disability support team at the regional benefits office in Northport. I read through claims and medical evidence, pull out what matters, and write a summary for the decision maker. I'm 27 and nine months in, and I'm honestly still slow at reading doctors' letters. Our waiting list is 14 weeks, which means people wait three months to find out if they can pay for their wheelchair repairs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how do you get through the parts you find hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI for loads of things outside work, every day, like getting it to explain a rule in plain words on my phone on the bus. I never put anyone's details in, obviously, that would get me sacked. I live in a shared flat with two friends, and I spent my savings on a laptop last year, so I've got about a week's money spare. My manager, Hollis, calls me the team's gadget girl, which I pretend to hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what a shame, honestly, because we needed the help. At work I'd say the 14-week wait isn't going anywhere then. Online I'd probably post something like: the hype was never the problem, the underfunding was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing gets easier. My job's safe, which is good with a week of savings, but I'd still be drowning in medical letters and still slower than everyone else. I was half hoping a tool would help me catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the small tools I'm allowed, like the summary feature in our email. I'd ask Hollis if I could test anything new the department brings in, even if it's tiny. Money-wise I'd try to rebuild a month of savings by not eating out with the flat on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Disappointed more than worried. A bit stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were hoping a tool would help you catch up. Is being slow something that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, quite a lot. There's a probation review in March, and my manager Hollis already said my numbers are low. If AI doesn't help, I just have to get faster the old way, which means taking letters home, which I'm not supposed to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for the waiting list in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, for not hiring enough of us. A tool was never going to fix a team that's been half-empty for three years. I'd rather they spent the money on two more caseworkers than on another pilot nobody uses.

say: I'd say the **14-week wait** stays, and underfunding was always the real problem.
I'd post that the **hype was never** the issue, staffing was.
think: My job is **safe**, which matters with only a week of savings.
I was hoping a tool would help me **catch up**, and now it won't.
do: Keep using the **email summary** tool and ask to test anything new.
Rebuild **a month of savings** by skipping Friday meals out with the flat.
S0.quote: A tool was never going to fix a team that's been half-empty for three years.
fieldNote: Unusually, she's **sorry AI stalls**, because she hoped it would help her keep up.
Her real pressure is a **probation review** in March with low numbers.
She blames **government underfunding** for the waiting list, not the tools.
Savings of **one week** keep even a safe job from feeling comfortable.

steps.text: Keep reading claims and push her numbers up before the March review
Ask Hollis to let her test any new department software
Skip Friday meals out to rebuild a month of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, if they use it to clear the waiting list and not to clear the staff. At work I'd be the first to volunteer for the new system. Online I'd argue for keeping the jobs and cutting the waiting time, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do all right in that one. Summarising medical evidence is exactly what these tools are good at, and I already use them more than anyone on my team. I think the job turns into checking what the AI wrote, and I'd be quick at that. But I'm not naive, they'll want fewer of us, and I'm still on probation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd write Hollis a one-page idea for a trial where the AI drafts summaries and we check them. In the first year I'd try to become the person who trains the others, because that makes you hard to let go. I'd also go to the union meeting, even though I've never been, because someone has to argue for the people who aren't gadget girls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a bit guilty about being excited. I sit next to Margaret, who's been here 20 years and hates computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Margaret. What happens to her in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Margaret knows every rule by heart but types with two fingers. If the job becomes checking AI drafts on a screen, she'll hate it and she might leave. I'd want to help her, but I also know I'd be one reason the old way disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they'd want fewer of you and you're on probation. Isn't that a real risk for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, yes. If they cut before I've proved myself, being keen won't save me. I'd still rather be the keen one than the one hiding at the back hoping nobody notices.

I'd argue online for **keeping jobs** while cutting waits.
think: Summarising evidence is **exactly what AI does**, and I already use it most.
I'm still **on probation**, so fewer staff could still mean me.
do: Write Hollis a **one-page trial plan** for AI-drafted summaries.
Become the person who **trains colleagues** on the new system.
Attend my **first union meeting** to speak for less tech-confident staff.
feel: She feels **excited** and a little **guilty** about it.
S1.quote: My colleague Margaret knows every rule by heart but types with two fingers.
fieldNote: She expects to **gain**, not lose, but knows her **probation** is a real weak spot.
Her guilt over **Margaret** shows she sees who pays for change.
She'd **bring AI in** herself, proposing the trial to her manager.
Joining the union for others is a **new step** for her.

steps.text: Become the team's trainer on the new AI case system
Send Hollis a one-page plan for AI-drafted evidence summaries
Go to her first union meeting to speak for older colleagues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to build something fair or we'll regret it for decades. I'd be loud online about a basic income, paid for by the companies that make this stuff. At work I'd tell people to talk to the union today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even my clever plan of being the AI checker dies. If the AI is as good as a person at thinking work, nobody needs a junior checking it, they'd keep one senior to sign things off. I'd be out within a year or so of it arriving, with a week of savings. That's not a plan, that's a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd start freelancing on the side, writing easy-read guides for charities, which I already do for free for the disability group I volunteer with. I'd use AI to do it fast and charge a small fee. If the office job went, I'd probably move to my sister's in the capital, where there's more of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, under the excitement. I keep thinking about rent day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use these tools every day. Does it feel different when they come for your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely different. I loved them as a helper. As a replacement, they make me feel like I trained my own successor on the bus every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come about three years later here. Does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for my job, there's nothing hands-on in it at all. It matters for the people on our list, though. Carers might keep their jobs a bit longer, but the disabled people I help could get robot help at home, which might actually be wonderful. I'd hold both those thoughts at once.

say: I'd call it the moment to build a **fair system**, like a basic income.
I'd tell colleagues to talk to the **union today**.
think: If AI matches people, nobody needs **a junior checker**, so I'm out.
With **a week of savings**, losing the job is an immediate problem.
do: Start paid **freelance easy-read guides** for charities using AI tools.
Move to **my sister's** in the capital if the office job goes.
Campaign online for a **basic income** funded by AI firms.
feel: She feels **scared** under her excitement, thinking about **rent day**.
S2.quote: I loved them as a helper. As a replacement, they make me feel like I trained my own successor on the bus every morning.
fieldNote: Her adaptive edge **vanishes** once AI no longer needs junior checkers.
She turns her **volunteer skill** into an instant side income plan.
She sees **robot help** at home as a possible gain for disabled claimants.
With **a week of savings**, moving in with her sister is the backstop.

steps.text: Charge charities a small fee for AI-assisted easy-read guides

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to make sure the waiting list disappears and the people don't. At work I'd keep pushing to be part of how it's brought in. Online I'd share anything about retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me a real shot. I'd spend two years as the AI person on my team and then move into designing how these services work, the bit where you sit with disabled people and ask what actually helps. That's thinking work too, so it goes in the end, but it's a few more years and it's a better job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, I'd sign up for a short evening course in service design that the council runs. I'd keep doing the easy-read work on the side and start charging for it by next summer. And I'd stop buying gadgets, which is hard for me, and get three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. With a knot in my stomach about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd be out within a year in the fast version. What's different here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to stop being junior. In two years I'm still the new girl. In five, I could have a real skill and some money behind me. People hire someone with a story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your flatmates about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to stop pretending it isn't happening. My flatmate Jonas (a junior accountant) laughs at me, but his job is even more screen work than mine. I'd send him the course link and nag him until he signs up.

I'd share any news about **retraining money** online.
think: Five years gives me **a real shot** at a better job.
Service design is still **thinking work**, so it buys time, not safety.

Start **charging for easy-read work** by next summer.
Stop buying gadgets and save **three months** of expenses.
feel: She feels mostly **hopeful**, with a **knot** about 2031.
S3.quote: In two years I'm still the new girl. In five, I could have a real skill and some money behind me.
fieldNote: The extra years let her **stop being junior**, which is her core weakness.
She knows her new path is **still exposed** to AGI later.
She'd **nudge friends** like Jonas to move too.

steps.text: Take the council's evening service design course this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it right, and I'd hold the government to that. At work I'd be cheering for it, as long as the waiting list goes and the staff are retrained. Online I'd be the annoying optimist, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd make a whole career out of the in-between years. Service design, then maybe working for a disability charity on how AI support works at home. By 2036 I'd be 37 with real experience. Thinking work still goes in the end, I know, but I'd have the most time of anyone on my team to get somewhere new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the office another two or three years and actually get good at the job, which I'm not yet. Then I'd move into the charity world. I'd keep the easy-read work going on the side the whole time, so I always have a second thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. It feels like a puzzle I'd enjoy, not a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep a side income in every version. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my dad (a factory electrician) lost his job when I was 12, and he had nothing else to fall back on. I watched him sit at the kitchen table for a year. I never want to be one wage away from that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your job ends anyway around 2036, why not call yourself calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not stupid about it. I'll probably be fine, but fine isn't guaranteed when you've got a week's savings now. Ask me again when I've got a few months in the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd be out of a job with a week's savings and no time to build anything. What would help is retraining money and a basic income floor, so people like me can jump to something new without missing rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we should want this at all. I think a lot of good could come of it for the people on our list. My worry is that the gain goes to the companies and the people on our waiting list still wait 14 weeks.

headlineQuote: My worry is that the gain goes to the companies and the people on our waiting list still wait 14 weeks.
portrait: Elena, 27, summarises **disability claims** in Northport and is still slow and on probation.
She shares a flat, has about **a week of savings**, and uses AI every day.
She's progressive and **excited** by AI, proposing trials while worrying about older colleagues.
Fast AGI wipes out her plan; with time she'd move into **service design** and charity work.
Her **dad's job loss** drives her habit of always keeping a side income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: out of work with a week's savings and no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining money** and a **basic income** floor so she can switch without missing rent.
